entries.title: Can a massive Madonna help slow secularization in Poland?
entries.summary: Europe's largest statue of the Virgin Mary will be inaugurated on Saturday in the Polish village of Konotopie. What will the huge monument mean for the village and for the Catholic faith in Poland in general?
entries.content:
Poland

Can a massive Madonna help slow secularization in Poland?

August 14, 2026

Europe's largest statue of the Virgin Mary will be inaugurated on Saturday in the Polish village of Konotopie. What will the huge monument mean for the village and for the Catholic faith in Poland in general?

With its grain fields, meadows and lake, the countryside around the tiny village of Konotopie in central Poland is idyllic. Towering above all this is a monumental statue of the Virgin Mary.

Home to just 120 residents and situated about 160 kilometers (99 miles) northwest of the capital, Warsaw, the previously little-known village of Konotopie has been in the headlines for weeks now as a result of the massive statue.

The snow-white structure, which is visible for miles around, is over 55 meters (180 feet) tall. The statue itself is 40.6 meters high and stands on a 15-meter-high pedestal shaped like a crown that is intended to serve as a viewing platform.

The figure dwarfs Rio de Janeiro's famous statue of Christ the Redeemer, which reaches a total height of 38 meters including its base.

A 'pile of concrete' or a 'fantastic achievement'?

The statue will be officially inaugurated on Saturday, August 15, the feast of the Assumption of Mary, a major holy day in the Catholic calendar.

Although final construction work is still underway and the site remains fenced off and guarded, thousands of people — both pilgrims and sightseers — have been flocking to see it for months.

Opinion about the project is divided.

"It's a nightmare," one critic of the statue told the weekly magazine Newsweek, "a complete waste. Instead of investing that money in useful projects, they financed a giant pile of concrete."

"This Mary is absolutely beautiful. My utmost respect. A fantastic achievement," said one devout lady visiting the site, according to the right-wing conservative weekly Sieci.

Wealthy, devout benefactor

The benefactor behind the statue, 75-year-old Roman Karkosik, hails from a nearby village and is one of Poland's wealthiest individuals.

Nearly 40 years ago, when the shortage economy of socialism gave way to free-market capitalism after the collapse of communism in eastern Europe, Karkosik was a young graduate from technical high school.

He started out as a bartender, but moved on to buying and selling scrap metal, producing soft drinks and later became the first entrepreneur in Poland to manufacture plastic bottles.

Karkosik made a name for himself on the Warsaw Stock Exchange. Some journalists have compared his role in Poland to Warren Buffett's influence on Wall Street.

His fortune is estimated at roughly €442 million ($511 million), and he ranks 44th on Wprost magazine's list of Poland's richest people. He lives in an 18th-century manor in the town of Kikol, just two kilometers from Konotopie.

A 'gesture of gratitude'

Karkosik and his wife, Grazyna, avoid both public appearances and contact with the media.

The cost of the statue remains a closely guarded secret. Media reports speculate that the project may have cost as much as €23 million.

The Karkosiks have described the Marian statue as a "gesture of gratitude."

According to media reports, the devout businessman wanted to thank the Virgin Mary for his recovery from a serious illness. His two brothers, who were also successful businessmen, both died prematurely after illnesses.

This is not the first time Karkosik has provided money for a religious structure. Back in 2011, he funded the construction of a church at a nearby pilgrimage site.

Artist feared seeing the finished statue

"I was afraid to come to Konotopie to see what had become of my design in reality," sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski told Polish media. Worried that the hands and face of the Virgin Mary might appear distorted, Matejkowski only visited the site in July.

"I opened my eyes and was stunned. The Mother of God is opening her arms to embrace us," he said with satisfaction. "That was exactly my intention: for the figure to have a human character, to come toward us," he explained.

Matejkowski says the statue has the facial expression of his 11-year-old daughter and the delicate facial features of his wife.

Region hopes for economic boost

Konotopie is situated in one of Poland's economically weak regions. There are no major industrial employers here, and jobs are scarce.

Local leaders hope the Marian statue will stimulate economic growth.

"The monument is not only a spiritual landmark but also a strategic asset for the region. We expect it to attract more investors and tourists, which will benefit the local economy," Krzysztof Kowalewski of the authorities in the nearby town of Kikol told Polish media.

Mayor Renata Golebiewska has said that revenues at local restaurants and bars have already broken local records.

Not the first statue of its kind in Poland

Poland is well known for its monumental Christian structures.

Following Poland's transition to democracy in 1989, a massive basilica was built in the village of Lichen in central Poland, overshadowing even the cathedrals of Paris and Cologne in scale.

The basilica is 138 meters (453 feet) long, 77 meters wide, and features a dome with a diameter of 35 meters. It can accommodate 20,000 worshippers.

Since 2010, Poland has also been home to the world's tallest statue of Jesus. Located in Swiebodzin near the German border, the 36-meter-high statue stands on a 17-meter-high mound.

Rising secularization

Whether all these gigantic monuments can stop the ongoing secularization of Polish society, however, remains highly questionable.

Although Poland is still one of the most Catholic countries in Europe, public trust in the Church continues to decline.

For centuries, the Catholic faith was a key part of Polish identity.

In the 19th century, when the territory that now makes up Poland was not an independent state and was divided up among foreign powers, Catholicism played a major role in the resistance to Protestant Prussia and Orthodox Russia.

After World War II, despite ideological differences, the anti-communist opposition and the Catholic Church in Poland worked together against the communist dictatorship.

During this period, churches became refuges for persecuted dissidents, and several priests were murdered by the secret police.

Pope John Paul II, himself Polish, also played a significant role in the struggle against the regime.

Catholicism in modern-day Poland

Since Poland's transition to democracy in 1989, however, the Catholic Church has experienced a crisis similar to that seen across Europe.

According to a September 2025 survey conducted by the Polish polling institute IBRIS, only 35% of Poles still trust the Church, down from 58% in 2016. Distrust rose from 24% to 47% over the same period.

In 2026, the annual number of priests ordained in Poland fell below 200 for the first time since 2000. Church attendance has also been steadily declining, especially among young people.

Even a gigantic Madonna is unlikely to reverse that trend.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: NATO jets shoot down drone over Latvia
entries.summary: Jets have shot down a foreign drone over Latvia after it entered the Baltic state's airspace. Its origin remains unclear, but the incident adds to concern over repeated incursions along NATO's eastern flank.
entries.content:
Latvia

NATO jets shoot down drone over Latvia

August 14, 2026

Jets have shot down a foreign drone over Latvia after it entered the Baltic state's airspace. Its origin remains unclear, but the incident adds to concern over repeated incursions along NATO's eastern flank.

NATO fighter jets have shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace, the alliance and Latvian authorities said Friday.

Two Italian Eurofighters were scrambled and one destroyed the unmanned aircraft, while two Turkish F-16s were also deployed under NATO command.

What happened over Latvia?

Latvia's military initially issued an air alert and urged people in affected areas to remain indoors and seek shelter.

Authorities said the foreign drone entered Latvian airspace over the Balvi region as a result of Russian electronic warfare activity.

It was not immediately clear where the drone originated, and NATO said an investigation was underway.

Latvian authorities did not identify the drone as Ukrainian.

However, the reference to Russian electronic warfare raised the possibility that a Ukrainian drone targeting Russia had been forced off course by interference.

Ukrainian forces had attacked targets in northwestern Russia overnight, according to Latvian media.

Has this happened before?

Latvia and other NATO countries along the alliance's eastern flank have faced repeated incursions by drones since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

A stray drone was also shot down over Latvia in early June, while other Ukrainian drones heading toward northwestern Russia have previously entered Latvian airspace and crashed.

Romanian and Spanish fighter jets were also deployed on Thursday after drones entered Romanian airspace near Ukraine.

Why are Italian jets defending Latvian airspace?

Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania do not operate their own fighter aircraft, so NATO allies rotate responsibility for policing their skies.

The Italian Eurofighters involved in Friday's interception are based at Siauliai air base in Lithuania.

entries.title: Zambia suspends vote count after violence
entries.summary: Zambia has halted the counting and publication of election results after violence targeting poll workers and reports of stolen ballots. The electoral commission says it will reassess the suspension within 24 hours.
entries.content:
Zambia

Zambia suspends vote count after violence

August 14, 2026

Zambia has halted the counting and publication of election results after violence targeting poll workers and reports of stolen ballots. The electoral commission says it will reassess the suspension within 24 hours.

Zambia's electoral commission has suspended the counting and announcement of election results nationwide with immediate effect, citing violence directed at election officials.

The commission said ballot papers had also been stolen in some cases and that it would review the suspension within 24 hours.

Why has Zambia suspended vote counting?

The Electoral Commission of Zambia said the decision followed incidents of violence targeting polling staff.

It added that ballot papers had been stolen in some locations, though it did not immediately give details on where the incidents occurred or how widespread they were.

The general election is a major test for President Hakainde Hichilema, whose economic reform program has been weighed against widespread frustration over the cost of living.

Around 8 million people were registered to vote in the southern African country of about 22 million people.

Voters were also choosing members of parliament and local councillors at more than 13,500 polling stations.

Were there problems during voting?

Long queues formed before dawn at polling stations in Lusaka, with some voters gathering around makeshift fires as they waited.

Local observers reported delays and frustration at some polling stations because of poor voter guidance, confusion over voter rolls and crowd-management problems.

European Union observers were monitoring the election.

Hichilema came to power in 2021 after defeating longtime rival Edgar Lungu, who served as president from 2015 to 2021 and died in 2025. Lungu's political legacy still looms over the election, with Hichilema's main challenger Brian Mundubile leading an opposition alliance backed by many of the former president's supporters.

entries.title: Berlin's Russian House: A hub for propaganda and espionage?
entries.summary: The Russian House stands in the heart of Berlin. Critics have long said it's being used to spread propaganda for Putin's Russia. Now, French authorities have said it is being used by the Kremlin for espionage.
entries.content:
Europe

Berlin's Russian House: A hub for propaganda and espionage?

August 14, 2026

The Russian House stands in the heart of Berlin. Critics have long said it's being used to spread propaganda for Putin's Russia. Now, French authorities have said it is being used by the Kremlin for espionage.

The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations, it is the subject of fierce disagreements and has long been a bone of contention in Berlin.

The massive seven-story building covering an area of almost 30,000 square meters opened in 1984. At that time, back in the days of the East German state, its role was to celebrate friendship with the Soviet Union through concerts, film screenings and book readings. It even had its own small bookstore.

But now, more than 40 years later, French authorities have linked the building to possible activities by Russian intelligence services.

"In light of the measures taken against German cultural institutions and organizations, the federal government is comprehensively and continuously reviewing the legal basis of the Russian House under international treaty law,” said German Foreign Ministry spokesperson Martin Giese at a press conference in Berlin earlier this week. 

In response to a question from DW about the organization's future activities, Giese emphasized that there are two bilateral agreements between Germany and Russia regarding real estate matters that cannot be easily revoked.

"It is, so to speak, an agreement that governs both the Russian House here in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut that we operate in Moscow," Giese said. Any action taken against one would also have direct consequences for the other. 

German tax money for Russian propaganda?

The property on Friedrichstrasse belongs to Germany, yet the building is run by the Russian agency Rossotrudnichestvo, the Federal Agency for the Commonwealth of Independent States, Compatriots Living Abroad and International Humanitarian Cooperation.

Rossotrudnichestvo, whose primary purpose is to promote the Russian language abroad, currently has dozens of similar institutions worldwide. The German Foreign Office has repeatedly stated that the employees of the institute have diplomatic status in Germany.

Since 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the agency has been on the EU sanctions list. At the time, the EU justified this by stating that the agency's goal was to consolidate "a wider public perception of the occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian." 

Moscow still maintains that the Russian House is a place to celebrate the friendship between the two countries: "The Russian House is Russia's cultural embassy in the heart of Berlin," according to the Russian Embassy's website.

The events that take place there attract 200,000 visitors a year, according to Russian House organizers. Critics label them as propaganda.

Berlin media outlets have repeatedly reported on events at the in-house cinema where, for example, a Holocaust film was shown in which Ukrainian citizens were portrayed as Nazis.

In an interview in August 2025, Robin Wagener, a member of the Bundestag for the opposition Green Party, told DW: "It is time we recognized that this is not mutual cultural exchange, but Russian war propaganda in Germany."

Germany fears closure of Goethe-Institut in Moscow

The Russian House is owned by the Russian Federation, but the Federal Republic of Germany pays the property tax for the building on the basis of its legal obligation under the bilateral German-Russian agreement on property issues relating to cultural institutes.

Moscow and Berlin are also bound by the Intergovernmental Agreement on Cultural Cooperation, which was signed in December 1992 and entered into force in May 1993. It has a term of five years and is automatically extended for the same period unless one of the parties notifies the other at least six months before the expiration of the respective term.

Both agreements — regarding the property of the Russian House and the Goethe-Institut, as well as the cultural cooperation between Russia and Germany — remain in force even in the fifth year of Russia's war against Ukraine.

It is an open secret that the German government is shying away from conflict over the Russian House because it fears the Russian government could respond by closing the Goethe-Institut in Moscow.

The institute was already forced to significantly scale back its operations in Russia in May 2023, when restrictions were imposed on the number of German officials in Russia.

A few weeks earlier, the Goethe-Institut's bank accounts in Russia were frozen in retaliation after the Berlin Public Prosecutor's Office opened a preliminary investigation against the Russian House for violating sanctions and ordered the freeze of its accounts.

So far, the Goethe-Institut continues to offer digital language courses in Russia. The libraries at its branches in Moscow and St. Petersburg continue to receive the latest German literature despite logistical difficulties, as representatives of the institute assured DW earlier this year.

Direct Russian-German contacts have become virtually impossible

According the cultural agreement, the contracting parties welcome "direct contacts between social groups and associations, including trade unions, churches, religious communities, artists' associations and political, cultural and other foundations."

However, in recent years, several German foundations in Russia have been classified as "undesirable organizations."

This includes the foundations run by Germany's established political parties.

Anyone who cooperates with "undesirable organizations" faces criminal prosecution in Russia. This makes all direct contact provided for in the cultural agreement virtually impossible.

This article was originally written in German and first published in August 2025. It was updated and republished in August 2026 to reflect news developments.

entries.title: Why women are breaking men's endurance records
entries.summary: Sophie Woods has completed the 2,000-kilometer Via Alpina faster even than the fastest-ever man. DW explains why she is not the only woman breaking men's records in extreme sports.
entries.content:
SportsGlobal issues

Why women are breaking men's endurance records

August 14, 2026

Sophie Woods has completed the 2,000-kilometer Via Alpina faster even than the fastest-ever man. DW explains why she is not the only woman breaking men's records in extreme sports.

New Zealand runner Sophie Wood, who competes under her maiden name, Sophie Grant, recently accomplished something truly remarkable.

Running for 29 days across the Alps, from Trieste to Monaco, Woods covered around 2,000 kilometers (1,243 miles) while climbing a total of more than 100,000 meters (328,083 feet) – on an average of three to four hours of sleep per night.

This made her the fastest person ever to complete the Via Alpina. The 42-year-old ultra-runner finished the route more than seven days faster than the fastest man ever to do so.

"It gives me goosebumps thinking about it, to take the overall record is amazing," Woods told DW.

"I was there for the adventure. I didn't really want to be running for longer than a month, that was enough."

The longer the distance, the smaller the gender gap

Woods is not the only woman to have broken a men's record in endurance sports in recent years.

In 2026, Rachel Entrekin won the Cocodona 250, a race covering roughly 400 kilometers in the United States, setting a new overall course record.

A year earlier, Tara Dower ran the Long Trail in Vermont. a distance of about 440 kilometers, in 3 days, 18 hours, and 29 minutes, beating the previous men's record by 2 hours and 40 minutes.

In 2019, Germany's Fiona Kolbinger became the first woman to win the Transcontinental Race. Cycling nearly 4,000 kilometers across Europe, she finished just under eight hours ahead of the second-placed male rider. That same year, Jasmin Paris became the first woman to win the 430-kilometer Spine Race in Great Britain, shattering the previous course record by more than 12 hours.

A comprehensive analysis by RunRepeat and the International Association of Ultrarunners examined over five million results from more than 15,000 ultramarathons. The findings showed that the longer the distance, the closer women came, on average, to matching men's times.

In the events analyzed, on average, the men were still 11.1% faster. At the 100-mile mark, the gap narrowed to just 0.25%. At distances exceeding 195 miles, the women were on average 0.6% faster.

'We're good at solving problems'

So why are women able to keep pace—or better—when the physical demands increase?

Certain physiological factors may play a role. On average, women possess a higher proportion of fatigue-resistant Type I muscle fibers and rely relatively more on fat as an energy source during endurance activities.

The advantages men typically enjoy—such as greater muscle mass and higher maximal oxygen uptake—may be less decisive in ultra-long events than in shorter races.

"Probably we are better at burning fat, and therefore it makes us able to go longer," Woods said – before pointing to other possible factors.

"I think we're good at putting our egos aside. And I think we're good at solving problems."

Competing in an ultramarathon is about much more than who can run the fastest. There are key decisions to be made about sleep, nutrition and physical pain. That's where her team comes in.

"I just put my life in their hands," she said.

"You kind of control everything you can and then you just throw it into chaos and see what comes out in the wash."

As little as 90 minutes of sleep, 7,000 calories a day

The extreme physical strain was evident in her sleeping patterns – towards the end, she was sleeping as little as 90 minutes a night. When she simply couldn't go any further, she would lie down right next to the trail.

"You just curl up on the side in a little mossy glen and hope that no one thinks you've died," she said.

"The sleep deprivation was one of the hardest parts of the whole thing."

Her alarm would often go off again as early as three in the morning.

At the same time, maintaining her physical energy was a huge problem, with her team estimating that she was consuming between 6,000 and 7,000 calories a day – through sports drinks, soft drinks, as burritos, falafel wraps, sandwiches, pasta, and McDonald's food. She ate much of this while on the move.

In the Dolomites, heat and pain added to the challenge.

"I bawled my eyes out in the Dolomites," she said.

"I was really hot. I was really sore. I was really swollen. I was shuffling along and I was just like: I don't know if I can do this."

Despite it all, she carried on.

Women long neglected in sports research

Despite setting the record, Woods wonders what she and other women could achieve if their bodies were studied as thoroughly as men's.

"As a woman, you need to be very careful when you read these studies to actually see who they are studying, because often it will be 10 male cyclists," Woods said.

"We have just been left behind in all of the research for decades," she said.

"As women, we are fighting for crumbs in the sporting world. We are fighting for more coverage, we are fighting for more research, we are fighting for more sponsorship."

The fact that several individual men's records have been broken by women doesn't mean that women are inherently better endurance athletes than men. Men still hold many records and are, on average, significantly faster over shorter distances.

However, in an interview with the BBC, sports physiologist Nicholas Tiller described very long endurance events as "the great equaliser." 

Woods is simply not interested in who holds the advantage on paper.

"I think the bravest thing to do is to try," she said.

"Try the scary thing. It doesn't matter what happens in the end because at least you've tried."

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Germany news: Wildfire forces evacuations in western woods
entries.summary: Hundreds of villagers have been evacuated in the Eifel region after a wildfire spread close to a village. Meanwhile, farmers warn that drought and high temperatures could cause major crop losses. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Wildfire forces evacuations in western woods

Published August 14, 2026last updated August 14, 2026

Hundreds of villagers have been evacuated in the Eifel region after a wildfire spread close to a village. Meanwhile, farmers warn that drought and high temperatures could cause major crop losses. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Friday, August 14, 2026:

  • A wildfire near the Belgian border has forced around 1,800 people to leave their homes
  • Flames burned within 400 meters of one village
  • Amid high temperatures, farmers say drought could badly damage grain, potato, vegetable and feed crop harvests

Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first.

Skip next section Merz thanks emergency services fighting Eifel wildfires

Merz thanks emergency services fighting Eifel wildfires

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has voiced thanks to emergency services fighting the wildfires near the Dutch and Belgian borders. 

"Wildfires are burning in many parts of the country. I am being continuously updated on developments," Merz wrote in a post on social media. "Where ever it's possible, federal police and the military are providing assistance. I thank all the emergency services for their tireless endeavors, often to the point of exhaustion."

Skip next section Almost half of Bundestag sign up to new 'opt-out' organ donor model

Almost half of Bundestag sign up to new 'opt-out' organ donor model

More than 200 lawmakers in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, have signed up to a cross-party initiative seeking to change Germany's organ donor rules.

The proposal seeks to move from an "opt-in" system to an "opt-out" one. 

At present, people in Germany have to carry a donor card, register as an organ donor, or otherwise inform healthcare professionals of their willingness to donate in a legally binding manner before death. If they do not, and they are deemed potentially viable donors, sometimes their next of kin are asked to decide on their behalf — a traumatic and difficult decision in the midst of a bereavement. 

With donor rates consistently failing to meet demand, some medical professionals have long advocated a system where instead of declaring your willingness to donate, you are assumed to be a potential donor unless you specifically say you are not a willing participant.

A draft law has been put forward in the Bundestag — not as a government initiative but as a cross party conscience vote, typically for causes with only a narrow chance of success but which politicians nevertheless wish to put in the spotlight.

In this case, however, 245 lawmakers have already signed the motion, in a chamber with 630 politicians. If the bill could gather some more support during the parliamentary process, it might have a chance of progressing.

Parliamentary debate on the bill is scheduled after lawmakers return from the summer break.

Around 8,000 people are currently on donor waiting lists in Germany.

Skip next section WWII munitions complicate Eifel firefighting

WWII munitions complicate Eifel firefighting

Bundeswehr forces joined in the fight against a forest fire raging in the Eifel on Friday, adding two water transport helicopter to the operation aimed at extinguishing the Hürtgenwald blaze.

Complicating matters are the numerous munitions scattered across the area since the end of the second world war.

In an effort to safely expedite access to the area, the Bundeswehr also deployed two rescue tanks to clear munitions and cut fire roads.

"The terrain is very difficult, and because of the high concentration of ammunition," as local councilman Ralf Nolten (CDU) told Germany's dpa news agency, "we can't send individual firefighters in with firefighting backpacks," said Nolten adding, "We also heard the explosions" that went off overnight.

In the fall and winter of 1944 and 1945, the Hürtgenwald was the scene of heavy fighting between US and Nazi-German troops as US tanks sought to finish their push east into Germany to end the war.

The ferocity and scale of the fighting led US soldiers stuck there waiting for reinforcements and facing entrenched German defenses to dub it "the death factory."

Skip next section Car industry hemorrhaging jobs

Car industry hemorrhaging jobs

Germany's automotive branch is losing jobs faster than any industrial sector in the economy according to the Federal Statistical Office Destatis.

The automotive industry is second only to mechanical engineering when it comes to size, yet its employment numbers are now at their lowest since 2005.

At the end of the first half of 2026, 691,500 people were employed in Germany's leading industry, a drop of 42,300 workers, or 5.8%, within a single year.

Destatis said manufacturing employment fell by 2.7% overall but had fallen by 7.6% in the automobile sector. Smaller segments within the car sector fell by 10%, whereas manufacturers themselves registered a 6.1% drop in employment.

In May, Germany's Association of the Automobile Industry (VDA) warned that the sector stands to lose as many as 225,000 jobs by 2035.

Numerous German manufacturers, such as VW, Audi and Porsche, have all cut jobs in an effort to remain lean in the face of rising Chinese competition and punitive US tariffs.

Skip next section German hiker injured in Alps fall

German hiker injured in Alps fall

A 66-year old German hiker was seriously injured in a fall in the Austrian Alps on Friday according to authorities in Nesselwängle, Tyrol.

Emergency services say the man slipped and fell a few meters, losing consciousness before falling over a second, 40-meter-high (132-foot) cliff.

The man's daughter and others administered first-aid and contacted mountain rescue. He was airlifted to an Innsbruck hospital.

On Thursday, a 36-year-old German died in a fall in Zillertal, Tyrol. A few days earlier, a 74-year-old German similarly died from a fall in East Tyrol.

Skip next section Dramatic rescue in Berlin high-rise fire

Dramatic rescue in Berlin high-rise fire

Several people were injured Friday morning when fire broke out in a 21-story apartment complex in Berlin's Friedrichshain neighborhood, near the Ostbahnhof train station.

The blaze started on the 11th floor, say firefighters, and quickly spread to floors above.

A fire department spokesperson described the situation as "dramatic."

Witnesses say numerous residents stood at windows and balconies prepared to jump rather than be consumed by smoke and flames.

Although jump cushions were installed as a precaution below, these were not used and authorities say residents were retrieved from a stairwell with a rescue ladder.

Some 130 fire, police and emergency services personnel were in action before residents could be saved and the fire extinguished.

Smoke damage is said to have been extensive, causing at least five injuries, and leaving roughly 70 people to be cared for on site.

The cause of the fire is unclear, though police are treating it as a possible balcony fire.

Skip next section German military joins battle against Eifel wildfire

German military joins battle against Eifel wildfire

The German military has deployed firefighting helicopters to help tackle a major forest fire in the northern Eifel region of western Germany.

Two NH90 transport helicopters took off from Fassberg in Lower Saxony on Friday morning, according to the Defense Ministry.

The helicopters are equipped with so-called Bambi Buckets, collapsible containers carried beneath the aircraft to drop water over burning areas.

Each helicopter can release around 2,000 liters (about 530 gallons) of water during a single run.

Several hundred hectares of forest are burning close to the municipality of Hürtgenwald in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia.

The village of Gey has been evacuated after flames moved dangerously close to homes.

Germany's military has also recently used CH-53 helicopters to help fight forest fires in France.

Skip next section Farmers fear drought will wipe out this year's harvest

Farmers fear drought will wipe out this year's harvest

Farmers fear they could see harvests wiped out entirely by ongoing drought and unseasonably high temperatures, says German Farmers' Association (DBV) President Joachim Ruckwied.

"We expect below-average grain harvests, especially when it comes to wheat and rapeseed," he said during an interview with Germany's Redaktionsnetzwerk media group.

"As far as fall crops are concerned, the trend suggests we must expect significant yield losses here as well."

Potatoes, vegetables and sugar beets, as well as grain maize and soy could be affected.

Ruckwied warned that although farmers in the north could hope for "acceptable" if "below-average" harvests thanks to occasional rains, farmers in drier southern Germany could be facing "total harvest loss."

"What's becoming a problem, especially in southern Germany, is that feed crops aren't coming in," he added, noting that this would force farmers to slaughter animals earlier than usual.

The threat adds to the financial pressure farmers already face when it comes to buying seed, fertilizer and pesticides, says Ruckwied.

"The economic situation is brutal… on the one hand high investment costs, and on the other, lower market prices for agricultural products."

Skip next section Wildfire forces evacuation in western Germany

Wildfire forces evacuation in western Germany

Fire forced the evacuation of some 1,800 residents in the Hürtgenwald area of western Germany's Eifel region Friday morning as flames, fueled by shifting winds crept within 400 meters (a quarter mile) of the village of Gey. 

The village is about 45 kilometers (28 miles) southwest of Cologne and close to the Belgian border.

Officials declared a "mass damage situation" Thursday evening before evacuations were ordered around 4 a.m. local time (0200 GMT) Friday morning.

Residents were told to gather only their most important possessions — above all documents and medicine — when leaving. They were also instructed to wear masks if possible due to poor air quality and those needing assistance were told to call emergency services.

An emergency shelter was set up at a nearby schoolhouse.

Hürtgenwald, located in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia near the Belgian border, has an overall population of about 9,000.

Authorities say roughly 25 hectares (62 acres) of forest is currently burning there — an area equivalent to 35 soccer pitches.

Skip next section Germany sees rise in new business registrations

Germany sees rise in new business registrations

Germany saw a noticeable rise in new business registrations in the first half of this year. Around 352,400 new businesses were registered, up 8.3% compared with the same period last year, according to the Federal Statistical Office.

Of these, around 69,600 were considered businesses of greater economic significance — for example because of their legal form or because they planned to employ staff. That was 3.0% more than a year earlier.

At the same time, the number of complete business closures in this category fell by 3.8% to around 49,800.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

A wildfire has forced the evacuation of around 1,800 people in western Germany's Eifel region.

The fire spread close to the village of Gey in the Hürtgenwald area, southwest of Cologne.

Officials ordered residents to leave early on Friday morning.

Meanwhile, German farmers have warned that drought and unusually high temperatures could cause major crop losses this year.

Stay with us here for these stories and more of the things that Germany is talking about today.

entries.title: Hunger stones: The history behind 'if you see me, weep'
entries.summary: Centuries-old hunger stones are emerging as Europe's rivers recede. Among the most famous is the Decin hunger stone in the Elbe River with its cryptic message.
entries.content:
August 14, 2026

Centuries-old hunger stones are emerging as Europe's rivers recede. Among the most famous is the Decin hunger stone in the Elbe River with its cryptic message.

As Europe's rivers recede during periods of drought, long-hidden traces of the past have resurfaced.

Alongside Nazi-era shipwrecks, unexploded World War II bombs and prehistoric mammoth remains, some rivers reveal history literally written in stone.

One such inscription, in German, reads: "Wenn du mich siehst, dann weine" — "If you see me, weep."

These words are etched on a hunger stone in the Elbe River near Decin in Czechia, close to the German border.

Why 'hunger'?

Hunger stones, or "Hungersteine" in German, are riverbed boulders that usually stay underwater and hidden, but become exposed when river levels drop significantly during prolonged droughts.

Unlike a high-water mark, which records the highest water level, the hunger stone marks the lowest.

For centuries, communities carved dates or inscriptions onto these stones whenever the waters of rivers like the Elbe, Danube or Rhine receded dramatically. Some hunger stones bear lists of years, including 1616, 1746 and 1842.

In a 2019 study "Extreme Droughts and Human Responses to Them: The Czech Lands in the Pre-Instrumental Period," Czech historian and climatologist Rudolf Brazdil and his colleagues drew on chronicles, administrative records and other documentary sources to examine how drought-affected communities lived long before systematic weather measurements.

For people living along rivers such as the Elbe, low water created a host of problems. Barges carrying timber, grain and other goods struggled to navigate shallow channels, disrupting trade along one of Central Europe's vital transport routes. In severe cases, shipping had to be restricted or halted altogether.

And drought also meant crop failure, rising prices — and hunger.

More than just drought memorials

While hunger stones were often treated as symbolic reminders of drought, they've proven to be more than that.

A 2020 study published in the journal Climate of the Past found that many of the dates and markings on Elbe hunger stones closely matched documented periods of exceptionally low water. The researchers concluded that many of the inscriptions were intended to record how low the river had fallen, rather than merely commemorate drought years.

The study also documented drought year markings on the Decin stone dating back to at least the 16th century, underscoring that the famous inscription "If you see me, weep" of 1904 represents only one chapter in the hunger stone's much longer history.

A doomsaying stone?

Yet, its fame lies mainly in its seemingly foreboding message. Even its sighting during the more recent European droughts of 2020 and 2022 inspired media coverage, describing its message as "chilling", "grim" or a "harbinger of hard times." 

In his 2019 study "Die Botschaft der Hungersteine" (or "The Message of the Hunger Stones"), Bernd Gross drew on newspaper reports, postcards and local historical records to reconstruct the history of the Decin hunger stone and noted that its inscription may have been inspired by an older one.

Gross cited newspaper reports from the 1890s that described a hunger stone near Techlovice, upstream from Decin, that reportedly bore German inscriptions such as: "We cried — We cry — And you will cry."

The man most often associated with the Decin stone's inscription is F. Mayer, a local innkeeper and boatman and member of the Elbe shipping community.

According to Gross, Mayer had the now-famous phrase carved onto the stone during the drought of 1904, dated July 18, along with his name.

A celebrity of its time

At the time, newspapers referred to it as the Bodenbach or Tetschen hunger stone, after the neighboring towns that today form part of Decin. They reported on the exposed stone and its message, while contemporary accounts described thousands of visitors who went to see it.

Postcards featuring the hunger stone also circulated widely, spreading awareness of the site far beyond the Elbe Valley.

The Reichenberger Zeitung, in circulation from 1860 to 1938, reported on August 28, 1904: "Day after day, groups gather on the rock; everyone wants to set foot on it at least once. However, the markings carved into the sandstone are likely to lose their visibility due to this frequent trampling."

Visitors were reportedly intrigued not only by the inscription but also the earlier dates carved into the rock, recording drought years stretching back centuries.

The stone that nearly disappeared

Ironically, the drought of 1904 that put the Decin stone and its inscription on the map very nearly caused its destruction.

Local river authorities decided to remove rocks and other obstacles from the Elbe to improve navigation, and Gross' study states that there were concerns that the Decin hunger stone could be removed as well.

Following the intervention of the Tetschen Boatmen's Cooperative, which petitioned the imperial authorities, the stone was spared. News reports stated that officials agreed to route planned river works around it in order to preserve what was already regarded as a historic landmark of the Elbe.

And while other obstacles were removed from the river, the Decin hunger stone survived.

The stone's story did not end there. When another severe drought exposed it in 1911, Mayer's famous inscription was reportedly carved again, this time more deeply. Later in 1938, a Czech inscription was added alongside the older markings.

Together, these dates and inscriptions chart centuries of the stone's history and its role as a marker of exceptionally low water levels on the Elbe.

Edited by: Oliver Mojen

entries.title: UK: Nigel Farage beats a trash can in Clacton by-election
entries.summary: Nigel Farage reclaimed his Clacton seat with 63% of the vote, but his main rival, Count Binface, took over a quarter, as Farage skipped the count citing security concerns.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

UK: Nigel Farage beats a trash can in Clacton by-election

August 14, 2026

Nigel Farage reclaimed his Clacton seat with 63% of the vote, but his main rival, Count Binface, took over a quarter, as Farage skipped the count citing security concerns.

UK right-wing populist leader Nigel Farage won Friday's by-election in Clacton, regaining the parliamentary seat he resigned a month earlier to trigger the vote. 

He took about 63% of the vote, while his main challenger, comedian Jon Harvey running as trash-can-costumed "Count Binface," secured roughly 27% — his best result yet in eight election attempts. The turnout was 44%.

What triggered the Clacton by-election?

Reform UK's Farage called the special election to prove his voter support amid a parliamentary investigation into an undeclared £5 million ($6.75 million, €5.85 million) gift from Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. Britain's major parties boycotted the race, calling it a self-serving stunt. This left Farage facing 33 mostly independent and novelty candidates.

Farage skipped the official vote count, saying police warned him of an "organized campaign to disrupt" the result. Essex police disputed reports of a credible threat but said a "proportionate and robust" security operation was in place. He also canceled a planned victory speech.

"I am damned if I am going to stand on a stage, having won a resounding victory... and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies," he told supporters.

What happens next?

The win doesn't resolve Farage's political troubles. The parliamentary standards investigation, paused when he resigned, is expected to resume and could still force him from his seat. Farage says the money was a personal gift he wasn't required to declare.

Last month, ​a Survation poll put Farage's share of the vote at 73%, a figure he fell short of. It comes as Reform UK's national polling is also slipping behind a resurgent Labour Party under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Who is Count Binface?

Count Binface is the alter ego of Harvey, a British comedian, writer and producer who uses the character to satirize UK politics.

He is a self-styled "intergalactic space warrior" who campaigns wearing a trash bin on his head. While he was expected to receive a large share of the vote, the figure was not expected to exceed 20 percent.

Binface has become somewhat of a serial candidate, challenging prime ministers past and present in line with a long tradition of novelty candidates in UK politics.

With the other parties boycotting the election, he became Farage's default rival with a comical platform vowing to "cut your taxes, and raise everyone else's," build one affordable home and nationalize singer Adele.

"The moral victory is already mine," Harvey, aka Binface, told the AFP news agency at the counting center ahead of the final count.

entries.title: India news: 7 dead, 3 trapped in Uttarakhand tunnel collapse
entries.summary: A rescue operation is continuing after a tunnel disaster in India's Uttrakhand state. And the results of a probe into an Air India flight that suffered a 300-foot drop are out. DW has more.
entries.content:
Published August 14, 2026last updated August 14, 2026

A rescue operation is continuing after a tunnel disaster in India's Uttrakhand state. And the results of a probe into an Air India flight that suffered a 300-foot drop are out. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here are the latest developments from India on Friday, August 14:

  • Seven workers have died in Uttarakhand after a landslide sent water and debris gushing into an under-construction tunnel.
  • Rescuers are trying to reach three workers still trapped inside.
  • Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami visited the site on Friday.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Football: Tata Steel sells Jamshedpur FC for $1

Football: Tata Steel sells Jamshedpur FC for $1

Tata Steel on Friday sold its entire stake in the top-flight football club Jamshedpur FC to Churchill Brothers, a Goa-based club, for a nominal 100 Indian rupees (€0.91, $1.05).

It comes two weeks after Tata Steel, one India’s biggest conglomerates, announced it was bowing out of the Indian Super League.

Jamshedpur FC players and fans had earlier appealed to Tata Steel to rethink closing down the club.

Churchill Brothers are set to take over the contracts of all Jamshedpur FC players and coaching staff with effect from September 2026, a statement from Tata Steel said.

"We are glad that this agreement gives our players and coaches the opportunity to continue playing club football," DB Sundara ​Ramam, Tata Steel's vice president of corporate services, said in the statement.

Skip next section Cricket: India to play 600th Test match on Independence Day

Cricket: India to play 600th Test match on Independence Day

India captain Shubman Gill said it was a "huge honour" to lead the Indian men's cricket team for the country's landmark 600th Test match as they play against Sri Lanka on Saturday in the opening match of a two-Test series.

The match coincides with the anniversary of India's independence from British colonial rule an August 15, 1947,

"It's a big honour and privilege for me to captain India in any Test match," Gill told the media in Sri Lanka's Galle.

"Captaining India in our 600th Test is a huge honour and doing it on India's Independence Day makes it even more special."

India played its first Test format of the sport in 1932 against England at the Lord's Cricket Ground in London.

Only two nations — England with 1,097 matches and Australia with 883 — have played more Tests than India.

Skip next section India electronics company investigates supply chain after child labor uncovered at supplier — report

India electronics company investigates supply chain after child labor uncovered at supplier — report

Indian home appliances firm Eureka Forbes said it has begun an internal probe ‌into its ⁠supply ⁠chain after authorities found child labour at one of its suppliers in New Delhi, the Reuters news agency reported on Friday.

According to Reuters, this week the country's National Human Rights Commission asked Eureka Forbes, along with electrical equipment ​maker Havells and Unilever's India unit to carry out a check of their supply chains.

Four children — aged between 14 and 16 — were rescued by Delhi authorities from a small electrical wiring and component company called YY Harness on Monday, Reuters reported.

"We take these allegations extremely seriously...we have initiated an immediate review and audit of the practices," Eureka Forbes Chief Financial Officer Gaurav Khandelwal told Reuters.

Hindustan ​Unilever denied having the small-scale vendor as a business Partner, Reuters said in its report.

Skip next section WATCH — Why insurance could help India's poorest beat the heat

WATCH — Why insurance could help India's poorest beat the heat

As Delhi's heatwaves intensify, some workers are using a heatwave insurance that pays out in extreme heat

In the southern Indian state of Tamil Nadu, a lone man's mission to grow a forest along the Thamarabarani River helped stop sand mining, protect water resources and safeguard his village.

Find out more in the latest edition of Eco India:

Skip next section India dispatches first tranche of relief supplies to quake-hit Colombia

India dispatches first tranche of relief supplies to quake-hit Colombia

India on Friday sent a first batch of a 20 metric-ton consignment of relief supplies for earthquake that struck Colombia, Indian foreign minister S Jaishankar said in a post on X.

"The assistance includes medicines & medical equipment, temporary shelter & hygiene support, and other essential items needed in the aftermath of the disaster," he said.

A magnitude 7.4 earthquake rattled Colombia on Monday in what was the Latin American nation's strongest quake in decades.

As per official figures, the disaster has left 265 dead, hundreds missing, and tens of thousands displaced across western Colombia.

Skip next section Delhi: High Court, airport and some government offices receive hoax bomb threats

Delhi: High Court, airport and some government offices receive hoax bomb threats

Delhi's High Court says it has received a bomb threat by email, prompting a bomb disposal squad and sniffer dogs to screen the court premises, Indian media reported.

Delhi High Court Bar Association (DHCBA) Joint Secretary Kunal Malhotra told news agency ANI that the threat appeared to be fake and the situation was under control.

The email threat mentioned a blast at the court at 2:11 p.m., news agency PTI cited its court sources as saying.

According to ANI, the Delhi Fire Service received calls of bomb threats in at least five additional locations including, Terminal 3 of the Indira Gandhi International Airport and other government complexes.

Authorities declared all threats to be hoaxes.

The bomb scare comes as security remains beefed up in the Indian capital ahead of Independence Day celebrations on Saturday.

Skip next section Air India Phuket-Delhi plane lost flight controls for four seconds, says Airbus probe

Air India Phuket-Delhi plane lost flight controls for four seconds, says Airbus probe

An Air India Airbus A320 that suddenly lost altitude on August 4 recorded losses in all three hydraulic systems, briefly losing crucial flight controls, media reports on Friday cited an initial Airbus analysis as saying. 

Air India flight AI2379 from Thailand’s Phuket to New Delhi had dropped 300 feet during cruise over the Indian state of Odisha, before recovering and landing safely in Delhi.

Twenty passengers and four crew members were injured during the incident which was classified as "serious" by Indian aviation authorities. 

India’s ​Aircraft Accident Investigation ‌Bureau is probing the incident with technical assistance from Airbus and France's BEA.

What do the Airbus findings say?

Airbus shared the technical evaluation after decoding the flight data recorder in a communication to Air India in response to the Indian flag carrier’s request for an assessment .

The plane’s elevators and ailerons, which control ​its pitch and roll, were unavailable for about four ​seconds, ‌during which the aircraft pitched upward, Reuters cited Airbus as saying in its preliminary findings.

The first officer applied a full nose-down input during the timeframe but ​there was "no direct response" from the flight-control surfaces, Reuters cited the assessment as saying, adding that the hydraulic systems recovered within seconds.

The initial analysis has not established a root cause and Airbus has asked Air India to conduct checks on ​the aircraft’s systems and sensors and to provide more information about the incident.

Airbus has also asked Air India to share the recent maintenance history of hydraulic systems along with more detailed accounts from the pilots.

There was no statement from the planemaker and Air India on the assessment.

Earlier this week, Indian media reports said that the primary captain of the flight tested positive for marijuana in a confirmatory drug test.

On Thursday, an internal communication from Air India showed that the carrier would now conduct a mandatory dope test for all its pilots, expanding checks beyond regulatory requirements.

Under the current rules, airlines in India randomly test at least 10 percent of their flight crew for psychoactive substances each year.

Skip next section Seven killed in Uttarakhand tunnel mishap, three missing

Seven killed in Uttarakhand tunnel mishap, three missing

At least seven workers have died in a tunnel collapse in the northern Indian hill state of Uttarakhand, officials said on Friday, adding that a search was underway for three missing people.

The incident occurred overnight when a landslide sent water and debris streaming into an under-construction tunnel belonging to Tehri Hydro Development Corporation Limited (THDC) in Pipalkoti, in Chamoli district.

According to officials, 22 workers were inside the tunnel at the time of the disaster.

The injured are undergoing treatment.

A multi-agency effort is underway to reach the three workers still trapped inside the tunnel, with teams from the National and State Disaster Response Forces, the Indo-Tibetan Border Police and fire services at the site.

Rescuers are battling rising water and debris during the search, as the state has seen heavy rainfall in recent days.

Visuals circulated by local authorities show rescue teams wearing head-mounted torches and using makeshift rafts to reach the flooded section of the tunnel.

Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami visited the collapse site on Friday morning and reviewed the rescue operations.

"Evacuating every worker safely is our topmost priority," Dhami said in a statement.

In 2023, a tunnel collapse in Uttarakhand left 41 workers trapped for 17 days before they were rescued.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you our daily news capsule with the biggest developments making headlines in India.

A tunnel accident in the northern state of Uttarakhand has left at least seven workers dead. A frantic search is underway for three missing workers as heavy monsoon rains batter the region.

In other news, the woes of the country's flag carrier, Air India, appear to be mounting. An Airbus A320 flying from Phuket to Delhi suddenly lost altitude earlier this month. The pilot in command later tested positive for marijuana. A preliminary analysis by Airbus has now found that the aircraft lost key flight controls for about four seconds.

India is gearing up to celebrate its 80th Independence Day tomorrow. A full-dress rehearsal for the Independence Day parade, held at the historic Red Fort in the Indian capital, has concluded.

Stay tuned as we bring you more.

entries.title: Can childhood trauma be prevented with a drug?
entries.summary: Researchers in Munich and Stockholm blocked the lifelong social cost of early adversity in mice with a single compound. The catch: it only worked when given during the trauma, not after.
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

Can childhood trauma be prevented with a drug?

August 14, 2026

Researchers in Munich and Stockholm blocked the lifelong social cost of early adversity in mice with a single compound. The catch: it only worked when given during the trauma, not after.

Trauma is usually treated as something you carry, manage, work through and sometimes ease. Rarely as something that could be stopped before it takes hold. That is what a group of researchers in Munich and Stockholm set out to test.

They began by making the first days of life hard. Mother mice were given far less nesting and bedding material than normal. That was enough to make mothers erratic, and the first days of life unpredictable. The mice raised in that hardship grew up looking perfectly healthy — with no obvious illness or anything visibly wrong.

Then researchers put them in groups and watched what happened. Repeatedly, these mice ended up at the bottom. Pushed into the lowest ranks of their social hierarchies, first as adolescents, then again as adults. A difficult infancy had left no visible mark — but it had set the position they would occupy for the rest of their lives.

When the researchers gave some of them a drug, the pattern disappeared.

The study, published in June, was led jointly by Mathias Schmidt at the Max Planck Institute of Psychiatry in Munich and Juan Pablo Lopez at the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm.

How does childhood trauma affect the brain and body?

Start with cortisol, the body's main stress hormone. When something stressful happens, cortisol floods the system. This is a standard, protective response.

What matters just as much is the off switch. The body needs to register that the danger has passed and wind the response back down. It does this through cortisol receptors — the parts of cells that detect the hormone and signal the system to stand down.

A protein called FKBP51 controls how sensitive those receptors are. Early hardship, the research suggests, causes the body to produce too much of it. That makes the receptors harder to trigger, so the signal to stand down never fully lands, and the stress response stays switched on far longer than it should.

Schmidt's point is that none of this is something a person can feel.

"Your cortisol response is something you don't feel," he said. "You may think you're very stress resilient, but your body is pumping out cortisol, and you don't know."

Can a drug block the effects of a difficult childhood?

The researchers used a compound called SAFit2, which blocks FKBP51. Given to the mothers during the stressful period, it reached the offspring through breast milk.

The treated mice went on to perform identically, within their social groups, to mice that had experienced no adversity at all — the social cost of a hard start erased.

The effect showed up in the brain as well as in behavior. The team screened gene activity across six stress-related regions and found that early adversity had left a broad imprint across them. The drug largely reversed it, most clearly in two: the medial prefrontal cortex and the nucleus accumbens, regions involved in emotional control and reward.

Can childhood trauma be reversed?

Not on this evidence.

In the Munich study, the compound was given during the stressful period itself, not after. What the study demonstrates is prevention, not repair.

Other studies have shown behavioral effects when the drug is used in adult animals, but full reversal of trauma already in place remains unproven. And prevention only works if you can identify who's at risk before the harm is done — a problem this research doesn't address.

Would this drug actually work on humans?

It's too early to say.

The study tested male mice only, so it is not yet known whether the same holds in females. And SAFit2 remains a research compound 3 effective in animals but not yet developed or safety-tested for human use. Still, Schmidt sees a realistic path toward clinical application within the next decade, noting that stress mechanisms are "very, very similar in animals and humans."

How is trauma treated now, and why doesn't it always work?

Existing treatments for stress-related disorders, including PTSD and trauma-linked depression, rely heavily on selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. These drugs target serotonin pathways. They work for many patients, but the mechanism is not fully understood, and a significant portion of patients don't respond at all.

By contrast, targeting FKBP51 would mean treating the pathology at its source. "We would actually not only be treating the symptoms, but also the cause of the disorder by acting directly [on] a stress mechanism," said Schmidt. "These types of drugs are currently not on the market."

Longer-term, Schmidt envisions a more targeted approach: identifying individuals who are genetically vulnerable to stress, whose FKBP51 expression is already elevated, and treating that group specifically after acute traumatic events.

On the other end of the spectrum are people who, through genetics or prior experience, prove remarkably resilient even under extreme conditions, and may not need medication at all. Understanding who does need it, Schmidt said, and reaching them in time, is where the research is heading next.

What are the signs of unresolved trauma?

Schmidt is careful that trauma is highly individual, psychologically and physiologically. The rough guide he offers is duration, not intensity.

A strong stress reaction immediately after a car crash or a violent event is considered normal — the body doing its job. What concerns clinicians is when the response persists well beyond that: still unable to cross a street a month later, still unable to sleep six weeks on. Those are his illustrative examples rather than diagnostic thresholds, but the principle holds. If a stress response isn't fading, it's advisable to speak to a doctor.

That remains practical guidance for now. The drug, if it ever exists, is at least a decade away — and on current evidence, it would need to come before the damage, not after.

Editor: Kaukab Shairani
